passage:
Since her father, Vikas, had stopped leaving for the office in the mornings, Sunaina, ten, had stopped asking about it. When a friend in the Andheri building lift asked why he was home so much, Sunaina said, "He's working from home. We're fine," and stared at the floor numbers.
At dinner Vikas began, "Sunu, you know the company—"
"I have maths homework," she said, and carried her plate to her room.
She lay awake past midnight watching the ceiling fan turn. Next morning she snapped at her little brother for using her pencil, then cried in the bathroom without knowing why.
At breakfast Vikas saw her red eyes and rested a hand on her shoulder. "After school, just us two. We'll talk."

qa.q: What reason did Sunaina give her friend for Vikas being home?
qa.a: She said he's working from home.

qa.q: Why does Sunaina escape to her room when Vikas starts to explain?
qa.a: Not hearing the details seems safer to her than facing the worry about her father's job, so homework becomes a way out.

qa.q: What choice did Vikas make at breakfast, and why might it help?
qa.a: He offered a private talk after school, giving Sunaina a safe, set time to hear the news gently instead of dodging it.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's little brother experience her snapping?
qa.a: He probably feels confused and hurt, since he only used a pencil and doesn't know the worry behind her temper.

grounding: A ten-year-old whose father has stopped going to work insists all is well and avoids the talk, while poor sleep and snapping show the strain.

passage:
"Uma, can we talk about my job?" Jaya asked, sitting on the edge of her daughter's bed.
"It's fine, Amma. I know. It's fine."
"The office closed my team. I'm looking for—"
"I said it's fine! Can you switch off the light?"
Jaya switched it off but didn't leave. "You've been awake late every night this week."
Silence. Then, very small: "Are we going to have to move?"
"Not now. And if anything changes, you'll hear it from me first."
"Okay." A long pause. "Sorry I shouted at Nikhil about the remote."
"I know, kanna. Worry makes everyone snappy. Me too."

qa.q: What happened to Jaya's team at the office?
qa.a: The office closed it.

qa.q: Why does Uma keep repeating 'It's fine'?
qa.a: Saying it's fine lets Uma avoid the details, which feel scarier than not knowing, even though the worry keeps her awake.

qa.q: Which of Jaya's choices opened the way to Uma's real question?
qa.a: Jaya switched off the light but stayed, and gently named the late nights, giving Uma room to ask about moving.

qa.q: How does Jaya seem to feel about Uma shouting at Nikhil?
qa.a: Jaya isn't angry; she understands that worry makes everyone snappy and admits she feels it too.

grounding: A girl whose mother has lost her job keeps saying it is fine and avoids the talk, while late nights and shouting show the strain.

passage:
This happened the winter I was eleven. Papa's shop closed, and I decided the best thing was not to ask. If anyone mentioned it, I said, "We're fine." I said it so often I almost believed it.
But I kept waking at three in the morning with my heart thumping. At school, when my friend Imran borrowed my eraser without asking, I yelled at him in front of everyone. He looked at me as if I were a stranger.
That evening I finally asked Papa, "Is it bad?" He told me the truth, in small pieces. It was hard to hear. But after that, I slept.
— Usha

qa.q: At what time did Usha keep waking up?
qa.a: At three in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Usha decide the best thing was not to ask?
qa.a: Not knowing felt safer than hearing bad news about Papa's shop, so saying "We're fine" kept the fear at arm's length.

qa.q: What turning point helped Usha sleep again?
qa.a: Finally asking Papa "Is it bad?" and hearing the truth in small pieces; facing it eased the worry that had been leaking out.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt being yelled at over an eraser?
qa.a: Imran was probably shocked and hurt, since the anger was far bigger than a borrowed eraser and he couldn't know about the shop.

grounding: A child looks back on insisting all was fine after Papa's shop closed, while waking at night and yelling at a friend showed the worry.

passage: Class teacher's note, Class 5A. Ojas (10) has been saying "Everything's fine, Ma'am" several times a day, even when nobody asked. His mother told me last week that his father lost his job a month ago. Since then Ojas has stopped asking questions in class, which is unusual for him. He yawns through first period and says he "just reads late." On Tuesday he snapped at his partner over a ruler and tore his own worksheet. When I asked gently how home was, he said quickly, "Papa is just resting. It's fine." I didn't push. I kept his routine steady and let him help in the library at lunch, where he relaxed. I called his mother to suggest simple, honest words at home, and asked our school counsellor to check in with him this week. — Trisha

qa.q: What did Ojas tear on Tuesday?
qa.a: His own worksheet.

qa.q: Why might Ojas keep saying "Everything's fine" when nobody asked?
qa.a: Not knowing or not talking about his father's job loss seems to feel safer than facing the worry, though the tension still shows.

qa.q: Which of Trisha's steps seems most helpful, and why?
qa.a: Keeping his routine steady and asking the counsellor to check in, while encouraging honest words at home, so he has support without being pushed.

qa.q: How might Ojas's partner have felt when Ojas snapped over the ruler?
qa.a: The partner was probably surprised and hurt, not knowing the snap came from worry about home.

grounding: A teacher notices a boy who says everything is fine after his father's job loss, while poor sleep and short temper show the strain.

passage:
Thursday
Mummy's office closed. That's all I know and I don't want to know more. When Kashish asked at the bus stop, I said, "Everything's fine, she's just taking a holiday." Mummy tried to talk to me after dinner. "Beti, come sit." I said I had homework and went to my room. If I don't ask, maybe it's not real.
But I couldn't sleep again. I lay there listening to the fan and to Papa and Mummy talking quietly in the kitchen. This morning I shouted at Kashish for taking my pencil, and it wasn't even my good pencil. She looked so hurt.
I'm not scared. I'm just tired.
Maybe tomorrow I'll ask Mummy one question. Just one. Like, will we still go to Nani's in May.
— Avni

qa.a: "Everything's fine, she's just taking a holiday."

qa.q: Why did Avni say she had homework when Mummy tried to talk?
qa.a: Not knowing felt safer than hearing worrying news, so she avoided the conversation even though the worry was still there.

qa.q: What small step is Avni thinking of, and why could it help?
qa.a: Asking Mummy one simple question, like whether they'll still go to Nani's, which lets her face the news a little at a time.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt when Avni shouted about the pencil?
qa.a: Kashish looked hurt, and probably confused, since it wasn't even Avni's good pencil and she didn't know about the worry at home.

grounding: A child's diary shows her insisting all is fine after her mother's job loss, while poor sleep and snapping show the tension.

passage: Exam week, and the power in their Kanpur colony kept going off. Uma sat on the steps with Jyoti, holding a torch over her notes. "Is your papa home in the day now?" Jyoti asked. "My mummy said his factory closed." "Everything's fine," Uma said quickly. "He's just on leave." She didn't want to know more. When Mummy and Papa talked in low voices, she turned up the radio. When they looked at her, she said, "I'm fine." But she hadn't slept well all week, and today she'd shouted at her little brother for touching her pencil box. Jyoti didn't push. She just shared her mango slice. Uma bit into it and stared at the torch beam, her jaw tight.

qa.a: "He's just on leave."

qa.q: Why does Uma turn up the radio when her parents talk quietly?
qa.a: She feels anxious and scared about what the news might mean, so not knowing feels safer than hearing the worry.

qa.q: How could Uma's parents help her with the worry leaking out?

passage: In their Pune flat, Aai had been home every day for three weeks now. Gautam knew the office had let her go; he'd heard it through the wall. He didn't ask anything. When his younger brother Tushar asked, "Why isn't Aai going to work?" Gautam said, "She's taking a break. It's fine." He said "it's fine" a lot. He stopped asking if they could get the cycle he'd wanted. At night he lay awake listening for the fridge hum. On Saturday Tushar knocked over his block tower and Gautam yelled so loudly that Tushar cried. Aai came in, looked at Gautam's face and sat on his bed. "You've been very quiet, Gautam. Do you want to ask me anything?" He shook his head. Then he nodded.

qa.q: How long had Aai been home every day?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Gautam keep saying "it's fine"?
qa.a: He felt worried and unsure, and saying everything was fine felt safer than facing the frightening news.

qa.q: What did Aai do that could help Gautam open up?
qa.a: She noticed his quietness and invited him to ask anything, gently giving him a safe chance to talk.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Gautam's yelling?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt shocked and hurt, not understanding that his brother's temper came from worry about Aai's job.

grounding: Shows a child whose parent has lost a job insisting all is fine and not asking questions, while tension leaks out in poor sleep and temper.

passage:
"Nandini, can we talk about my job?"
"Everything's fine, Papa. Don't tell me."
Bhupen sat down on the edge of her bed. "Beta, you've been saying that for two weeks."
"Because it is fine."
"You haven't been sleeping. I see your light on."
"I'm reading."
"And yesterday you shouted at Nani about the TV."
Nandini stared at her pillow. "If you tell me, it'll be real."
Bhupen was quiet. "It's already real. But you don't have to carry it. I'm looking for new work, and we're okay for now. You can ask me anything, any time."
Nandini's eyes filled. "Will we have to move?"
"I don't know yet. If anything changes, I'll tell you first."
She leaned against him.

qa.q: How long had Nandini been saying everything was fine?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What does Nandini mean by "If you tell me, it'll be real"?
qa.a: She feels frightened and anxious, and not knowing the details has felt safer than facing the worry.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say that could help Nandini sleep better?
qa.a: He told her she didn't have to carry the worry, that they are okay for now, and that she can ask anything, which gives her honest reassurance.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when Nandini shouted about the TV?
qa.a: Nani might have felt surprised and hurt, not knowing Nandini's temper came from worry about Papa's job.

grounding: Shows a child whose parent lost a job insisting everything is fine and avoiding questions, while worry leaks out in poor sleep and temper.

passage:
Last year, Papa lost his job at the factory. I heard him tell Ma in the kitchen. I didn't ask anything. When my friend Madhuri asked, "Is everything okay at home?" I said, "Totally fine."

I kept saying that. At school, at tuition, to myself. But at night I couldn't sleep, and I shouted at my little brother for nothing.

One evening Ma sat on my bed. "You've been cross. Are you worried about Papa?"

I started crying. I didn't know I was so scared.

Ma said, "It's okay to ask questions. We're looking for work, and we'll manage together."

I'm Bhavna. Not knowing felt safer, but it wasn't. Knowing, with Ma beside me, was better.

qa.q: What did Bhavna tell Madhuri when asked about home?
qa.a: Bhavna said, "Totally fine."

qa.q: How was Bhavna really feeling while saying everything was fine?
qa.a: Bhavna was scared and worried, which showed up as poor sleep and shouting at the brother.

qa.q: What did Ma do that helped Bhavna?
qa.a: Ma noticed Bhavna's crossness, gently asked about the worry, said questions were okay and promised they'd manage together.

qa.q: How might Bhavna's little brother have felt being shouted at?
qa.a: The little brother was probably hurt and confused, since he'd done nothing wrong.

grounding: A child whose parent lost a job says everything is fine and stops asking, while worry leaks out as poor sleep and temper.

Class teacher's note, Class 6, Thursday.

Yusuf has been different these past two weeks. He's tired in class, and today he snapped at Tejas over a pencil. When I asked if something was wrong, he said quickly, "Everything's fine at home."

Later his mother called. She told me his father had lost his job and Yusuf hadn't asked a single question about it.

I think not knowing feels safer to Yusuf, but the worry is showing up as tiredness and a short temper. I spoke to him gently after class, and I've let the school counsellor know. His mother and I agreed she'll talk with him this evening, simply and honestly.

qa.q: What did Yusuf snap at Tejas over?

qa.q: Why did Yusuf say quickly that everything was fine?

passage:
Wednesday night

Mum said Dad's company closed and he doesn't have a job now. She said it at dinner, very calm. I just said "okay" and went to my room.

I don't want to ask anything. If I don't ask, maybe it's not really true.

But I can't sleep. And today I yelled at Thomas at school for sitting in my seat. He looked so shocked. I don't even know why I did it.

Maybe I'm more worried than I think.

Tomorrow I'll ask Mum one question. Just one. Like, "Will we be okay?"

— Bidisha

passage: The week before Diwali, the sugar mill in their small town let Zubin's father go. At dinner, Papa explained it quietly. Zubin nodded, said, "It's fine, you'll find another one," and asked for more rice. After that he never asked about it again. When his sister Lavanya mentioned it, he said, "Everything is FINE," and left the room. But he lay awake counting the turns of the ceiling fan, and he snapped at the dog for barking and at Lavanya for borrowing his pencil. On Diwali night, Mummy sat on his bed. "You can ask me anything, you know. Not knowing can be scarier." Zubin turned to the wall. After a long time he whispered, "Will we be okay?"

But she couldn't fall asleep until midnight, and she shouted at Omar for taking the red marker, then cried in the toilets. Her teacher noticed and called her mother that afternoon. That evening her mother sat on her bed. "I'm looking for new work. You can ask me things." Ines pressed her face into the pillow. "I don't want to know," she said. Then, quietly: "Is it bad?"

passage: At the school's summer sports camp, Deepak was usually the loudest boy on the field. This week he was quiet, and then suddenly furious when he dropped a catch, throwing his cap on the ground. Vishal sir, the coach, found him later sitting by the water cooler. "All okay at home?" "Yes. Totally fine," Deepak said too quickly. "Papa's just at home now. Nothing's wrong." He hadn't asked his parents a single question since they told him about the job. "I'm not sleeping much," he added, then looked annoyed with himself. Vishal sir sat beside him. "Sometimes not knowing feels safer. But worries grow in the dark." That evening he called Deepak's mother, and the school counsellor met Deepak the next morning.

qa.q: Where did Vishal sir find Deepak?
qa.a: Sitting by the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Deepak say "totally fine" so quickly?
qa.a: He was worried and scared about his father's job, and denying it felt safer than facing it, though the tension showed in anger and poor sleep.
